title: Samantabhadra
hook: the bodhisattva of practice and great vows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Manjushri, and a silence that won the day. Your line was the sword of wisdom. Which knot did you cut with one true sentence? Day one thousand one hundred seven, and a new week.

When space itself comes to an end, my vow will come to an end. But space never ends, so neither will the vow. That, in paraphrase, is the refrain at the close of a vast Mahayana sutra, and the one speaking it is a bodhisattva named Samantabhadra. It's a promise with no expiry date. Not a resolution that fades by February. A vow as wide as the sky, repeated again and again until it sinks in. Today, the bodhisattva of practice and great vows.
screen: `WHEN SPACE ENDS, THE VOW ENDS.` → `SPACE NEVER ENDS.` → `NO EXPIRY DATE.`

segments.voice: First, the pair. In some Chinese temples the Buddha sits with a bodhisattva on either side: Manjushri on a lion, and Samantabhadra on a white elephant. Wisdom and practice, side by side. The elephant is a good mount for practice: slow, steady, very hard to push off the road. Second, the vows. The Flower Ornament Sutra, the Avatamsaka, ends with Samantabhadra setting out his great vows. In paraphrase, they run like this: to honor all the Buddhas; to praise them; to make offerings; to admit and turn from the harm one has done; to rejoice in the good done by others; to ask the Buddhas to teach; to ask them to stay in the world; to follow their example; to meet every being where they are; and to give away the merit of everything, for the good of all. After each one comes the same refrain about space and its endlessness. Third, the small one in the big list. Look at the fifth: rejoicing in the good done by others. It sounds modest. Being glad when a coworker gets the praise. Being glad when a sister's life goes better than yours. In the sutra, it stands right beside honoring all the Buddhas, and it gets the same endless vow. Practice, in this picture, includes the small, daily kinds. Fourth, the promise to others. In the last chapter of the Lotus Sutra, Samantabhadra arrives from far away and makes a promise of his own: whoever keeps and studies that sutra, he will come to them, riding his white elephant, to guard them and to teach them again any line they've forgotten. Practice, in that promise, is never quite done alone.
screen: `A LION AND A WHITE ELEPHANT.` · `VOWS THAT LAST AS LONG AS SPACE.` · `REJOICE IN THE GOOD OF OTHERS.` · `HE COMES TO THOSE WHO PRACTICE.` · then, large: `GREAT VOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Settle, and breathe. Look over the day ahead, or the week. Choose one small practice you could actually keep: a minute of quiet before picking up the phone, a kind word to someone you usually rush past, being glad out loud when someone else does well. Make it small enough to keep. Then, silently, in your own words, make it a vow. Not until space ends. Just today, and then today again. Rest with it, the way the elephant stands: steady, unhurried. The bell holds the time.
Samantabhadra. The bodhisattva of practice and great vows, riding a white elephant, whose vows last as long as space. Today's word.
Your line: great vows. Today, keep the one small vow you made, and when someone else does well, be glad for them out loud. Tomorrow, Maitreya. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism the vows of Samantabhadra are recited in temples and at home, and Samantabhadra is shown on a white elephant, often beside Manjushri on his lion.

myth: Samantabhadra's vows end when the work is finished
the refrain: when space ends, the vow ends, and space never ends.
one of the vows is to rejoice in the good done by others
it stands beside honoring all the Buddhas, with the same endless refrain.
in the Lotus Sutra, Samantabhadra promises to guard those who keep the sutra
he says he'll come to them on his white elephant.

fork.setup: you've taken on the vow to rejoice in the good done by others. then a friend lands the very thing you were hoping for. what does the vow ask?
options: wait to be glad until you get yours too
say nothing, so it stays even
fork.reveal: rejoicing in others' good is one of Samantabhadra's great vows, and in the sutra it gets the same endless refrain as honoring the Buddhas.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva of practice, called Puxian in China and Fugen in Japan.

trapdoor: what you thought: one more name in a long list of bodhisattvas.
what it means: the bodhisattva of practice, whose great vows, from honoring all Buddhas to rejoicing in others' good, last as long as space.
what a scholar hears: the vows that close the Flower Ornament Sutra, each with its refrain about space, and the white elephant of the Lotus Sutra's last chapter.

sources.ref: Avatamsaka Sutra, the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra (closing chapter of the Gandavyuha)
Lotus Sutra, final chapter (the encouragement of Samantabhadra)

notes: The vows are paraphrased in order from the 'Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra'; the count (ten) is not stated aloud, but the list given has ten items and 'the fifth' is rejoicing in others' merit. Confirm order and wording, especially 'to meet every being where they are' for 'to accord always with beings' and 'to admit and turn from the harm one has done' for repentance.
Refrain paraphrased: when the realm of space is exhausted the vow would be exhausted, but since space is inexhaustible, the vow is endless. Confirm.
The triad (Buddha, Manjushri on a lion, Samantabhadra on a white elephant) is said of 'some Chinese temples'; the Lotus Sutra's elephant has six tusks, left out.

Lotus Sutra final chapter: Samantabhadra promises to appear on a white elephant to protect and help those who keep the sutra, including restoring forgotten passages; confirm 'help them remember what they've lost'.
howItsDone says the vows are recited in temples and at home in East Asia; confirm.

Editor: 'help them remember what they've lost' changed to 'teach them again any line they've forgotten' (the Lotus Sutra's promise is about forgotten passages); the second 'in this picture' changed to 'in that promise' to cut a repeated phrase.
